strengths: This paper is of good written quality that makes the readers easy to follow. The logic, the notion expression, and the experiments are all very clear.
The asymmetric design is interesting and this design has been proven an efficient way to deal with resource-limited circumstances.
The experiments conducted are very convincing to support the contribution claimed by the authors. The properties of the proposed method are well demonstrated in the ablation study.

The paper addresses the challenges in Composed Image Retrieval by introducing the zero-shot composed image retrieval (ZSCIR). This method offers a fresh perspective on image retrieval by transforming it to a text-to-image format, thereby providing a more direct linkage between descriptive text and its corresponding image.

The introduction of an adaptive token learner, which effectively translates visual features into textual tokens, stands out as a major strength. This conversion mechanism is pivotal in enhancing the representation of images and ensuring that the retrieval process is both accurate and efficient. The adaptive nature of the learner means that it can adjust and improve over time, potentially leading to even better retrieval results in the future.
An asymmetric zero-shot composed image retrieval framework is proposed.
Global contrastive distillation and local alignment regularization techniques are proposed to align features from different models.
Overall, this paper is well written and easy to follow.

I like the motivation of this work since deploying original large foundation model is almost impossible in mobile applications. Different from pruning or distilling such heavy models, the authors proposed the lightweight encoder with a tunable adaptive token learner. The idea behind is borrowed from the LLM-Adapters.
The proposed modules are technically sound and the experimental resutls are sufficient. The training resources are extremly friendly with 4 RTX 3090 GPUs.
weaknesses: It could be better to discuss more about the number of token selections in detail. According to Fig 3, it seems the performance is a bit sensitive to the number of tokens used in the proposed method. Then, a more detailed discussion of this observation with a visual example of the same query but a different number of tokens could help to better demonstrate the impact brought by the tokens. Specifically, it is unclear how the token selection process balances the need for comprehensive visual information with the risk of introducing noise or redundancy. A more thorough analysis of the trade-offs involved in selecting different numbers of tokens, including the impact on attention maps and feature representations, would strengthen the paper.

It could be good to add a discussion of the relationship between the proposed adaptive token learner and the similar approach used in the following papers [1,2]. They have a similar structure, a discussion would help to better locate the position of the token learned in this work. While the paper mentions the token learner's role in extracting visual features, it does not adequately differentiate its specific function and contribution from existing token-based methods. A more detailed comparison of the architectural differences, training objectives, and the specific types of representations learned by the proposed token learner versus those in [1,2] is needed to clarify the novelty and unique aspects of this work.

While the adaptive token learner is a strength in terms of converting visual features to textual tokens, there's a risk that the system could become overly reliant on this component. If the learner fails or encounters unanticipated scenarios, it might compromise the effectiveness of the entire retrieval process. Specifically, the paper does not discuss the sensitivity of the token learner to variations in image quality, such as blur, noise, or changes in lighting conditions. It is unclear how the system would perform if the visual features extracted are not representative of the image's content due to these factors.

Introducing an asymmetric text-to-image retrieval approach, while innovative, adds an extra layer of complexity to the system. This might present challenges in terms of maintainability, debugging, and further development of the system. The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the computational overhead associated with maintaining two separate models (one lightweight for the query and one heavier for the database). It also lacks a discussion on the potential for increased latency or synchronization issues between these models.

The transformation of the retrieval problem from image-to-image to text-to-image inherently assumes that the descriptive texts are of high quality and detailed. Any inaccuracies or vagueness in the text could lead to inefficient or incorrect image retrievals. The paper does not address how the system handles ambiguous or poorly worded text descriptions. For example, if a user provides a very general description, it is unclear how the system would prioritize relevant images or if it would return a large set of potentially irrelevant results.
The paper presentation is not very attractive. It is difficult to understand the novelties / contributions after reading the introduction of the paper.
The clarity of the writing, particularly in the methods section, requires improvement.
For image-only retrieval, could you provide results using the DINO-V2 and MoCo-V3 pretrained models? The CLIP model is typically used for content matching between image and text features.

Since this work is a retrieval task, it is important to report how the retrieval performance varies as the gallery size scales up. I understand that the three evalutation datasets are standard benchmarks. However, it would make the contribution more solid if millions distractors could be involved in the gallery, although most existing SOTAs didn't report such results. Specifically, the impact of gallery size on both retrieval accuracy and computational cost should be analyzed. The paper should include experiments with varying gallery sizes, perhaps from the original dataset size up to a million distractors, to demonstrate the scalability of the proposed method. This is crucial for real-world applications where the gallery size can be substantial.

The inference time should be reported including in the query side and in the cloud side. It's critical to understand the latency introduced by both the lightweight query model and the large gallery model. The paper should provide a breakdown of the inference time for each component, including the time taken for feature extraction on the query side and the time for similarity calculations on the server side. This will help assess the practical feasibility of the proposed approach in real-time applications.
